# III. Why Mirroring Fails

The passive block cannot vote its own judgment under the proposal.[^1] It follows that the block's managers owe no duty of care when they cast the mirrored votes, so the fiduciary objection to mirroring collapses. For the same reason, the SEC has no basis to require disclosure of mirrored votes.[^2] Mirroring is therefore lawful under existing doctrine.

[^1]: Proposed Rule 14a-22, 90 Fed. Reg. 1201, 1204 (Jan. 6, 2025). Because the duty of care attaches only to a discretionary decision, and a fund that commits in advance to vote in proportion to other holders makes no decision at the time of the vote, the duty has nothing to attach to; a care claim requires a choice the fiduciary could have made differently, and a mechanical rule leaves none. The same absence of discretion means the vote is not the adviser's "voting decision" within the meaning of the disclosure rule, which applies only to votes the adviser determines.
[^2]: See Form N-PX, 17 C.F.R. § 274.129 (2024).
